newsitem.title: FRANCE: Juppe calls for unity in right ahead of '98 vote.
newsitem.headline: Juppe calls for unity in right ahead of '98 vote.

text.p: French Prime Minister Alain Juppe called on pro-government parties on Saturday to unite amid speculation that proposed electoral law reforms could see big gains for extreme rightist Jean-Marie Le Pen.

"Our voters who closed ranks massively in May 1995 to elect Jacques Chirac president would not forgive us if we went into the (spring 1998) general election in dispersed order," Juppe told a seminar of leaders of the centre-right Union for French Democracy (UDF) party.
The UDF is junior partner in the conservative cabinet led by the neo-Gaullist Rally for the Republic (RPR) from whose ranks both Chirac and Juppe emerged.
Juppe made no direct reference to electoral reform when speaking in this Atlantic coast resort but he confirmed it was in the air in an interview with the daily Le Figaro.
The suggestion, however, dominated all talk among politicians and was prominent in national newspaper headlines.

The reform, which would reintroduce some proportional representation into French elections, was mostly aimed at undercutting what increasingly looks like possible defeat of the RPR and UDF in the general elections in 20 months' time at the hands of the opposition Socialist party.
Opinion polls suggest Chirac's failure to live up to election-time promises of cutting unemployment and improving daily life will give the opposition a strong boost at the polls.

Newspapers said the introduction of some proportional representation would presumably result in the Socialists losing dozens of seats they could otherwise expect to win to the benefit of junior partners on the left.

But the probable price of reducing Socialist gains would also be the election to the 577-seat National Assembly of up to 40 members from Le Pen's stridently-xenophobic National Front (FN) party, according to specialists' calculations.
Under the current system, a candidate must win more than half the votes in the first round to be elected outright to the assembly. Otherwise the two top candidates go on to a run-off.
The system allows for deals between mainstream left-wing and right-wing parties, especially beneficial to the Socialists, but it shuts out the FN, shunned by mainstream politicians.

The FN failed to win a single seat in the last national elections, in 1993, despite winning 12.5 percent of the popular vote. The party, which wants to expel foreigners from France, is now credited with around 15 percent of voting intentions.

Bruno Megret, a senior National Front leader, welcomed possible electoral reform but said in a statement it showed how frightened the centre-right government was of his party's rise in public support.
Former Socialist prime minister Laurent Fabius joked: "When a majority changes the voting rules at the last minute, it shows what little confidence it has in its own chances at the polls."
"Union is a matter of conviction," Juppe said in La Baule. "I hope that the UDF, our equal partners in government, will join us squarely to prepare the 1998 vote."

Parliamentary floor leaders said that, under the proposed reform, deputies might be elected by proportional representation in the most populated regions while single-member constituencies remained in rural areas.
